newsitem.title: DUBAI: Petrochemicals seen blocking EU-GCC trade pact.
newsitem.headline: Petrochemicals seen blocking EU-GCC trade pact.

text.p: A strong petrochemical lobby in the European Parliament is blocking a free trade accord between oil-rich Gulf states and the 15-member European Union, the head of a European pressure group said on Monday.

"After nearly 10 years of talks between the two sides, the issue of protective tariffs in Europe against Gulf petrochemicals is still the main obstacle," said Jean-Michel Dumont, secretary general of the Parliamentary Association for Euro-Arab Cooperation.

"European industrialists have a strong lobby in the EU parliament. So far they have managed to block the free trade accord," Dumont, who is on a visit to the United Arab Emirates, told Reuters. He is organising a Euro-Arab conference on Middle East peace in Dubai due to take place in April.
Dumont said Gulf Arab states, eager to diversify their economies away from oil, were nurturing a growing petrochemical sector, which many Europeans see as a threat to their local industries.
"Unlike the Gulf Arab states, production costs in Europe are high. In this respect they (Europeans) cannot compete," he said.
Saudi Arabia produces about five percent of the world's petrochemicals. Other Gulf Arab states are also investing heavily in petrochemical plants.
EU countries impose heavy tariffs on petrochemical exports from the six Gulf Cooperation Council Council (GCC) states -- Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Oman and Qatar.
The two blocs in April agreed on a time frame of no more than two years to forge a free trade agreement, and Dumont said other issues blocking the treaty were being resolved.

"GCC states are about to unify tariffs, some of them are already World Trade Organisation members, others are about to join," he said. "With these issues resolved that only leaves the petrochemical issue."
He said his group, which represents 97 delegates in the 626-seat EU parliament, was working at various levels to bypass the petrochemical obstacle.

"The petrochemical lobby in Europe should realise that there is a price to be paid every time we sign a trade accord, in this instance it is the petrochemical industry that has to pay the price," Dumont said.

"But any sacrifices by the European petrochemical industry will be outweighed in the long run by benefits from the free trade accord," he said. "If this message gets through, we will see an accord by 1998."
